module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 978

*Reference:*
 - [erdosproblems.com/978](https://www.erdosproblems.com/978)
 - [Ho67] Hooley, C., On the power free values of polynomials. Mathematika (1967), 21--26.
 - [Br11] Browning, T. D., Power-free values of polynomials. Arch. Math. (Basel) (2011), 139--150.
 - [Er53] Erdős, P., Arithmetical properties of polynomials. J. London Math. Soc. (1953), 416--425.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Polynomial Set

namespace Erdos978

/-- Let `f ∈ ℤ[X]` be an irreducible polynomial with positive leading coefficient. Suppose that the
degree `k` of `f` is larger than `2` and is not equal to a power of `2`. Then the set of `n` such
that `f n` is `(k - 1)`-th power free is infinite, and this is proved in [Er53]. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_978.variants.sub_one {f : ℤ[X]} (hi : Irreducible f) (hd : 2 < f.natDegree)
    (hp : ∀ (x : ℕ), f.natDegree ≠ 2 ^ x) (hlc : 0 < f.leadingCoeff) :
    {n : ℕ | Powerfree (f.natDegree - 1) (f.eval (n : ℤ))}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- Let `f ∈ ℤ[X]` be an irreducible polynomial with positive leading coefficient. Suppose that the
degree `k` of `f` is larger than `2`, is not equal to a power of `2`, and `f n` has no fixed
`(k - 1)`-th power divisors other than `1`. Then the set of `n` such that `f n` is `(k - 1)`-th
power free has positive density, and this is proved in [Ho67]. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_978.parts.i {f : ℤ[X]} (hi : Irreducible f) (hd : 2 < f.natDegree)
    (hp2 : ∀ (x : ℕ), f.natDegree ≠ 2 ^ x) (hlc : 0 < f.leadingCoeff)
    (hp : ∀ (p : ℕ), p.Prime → ∃ n : ℕ, ¬ (p : ℤ) ^ (f.natDegree - 1) ∣ f.eval (n : ℤ)) :
    HasPosDensity {n : ℕ | Powerfree (f.natDegree - 1) (f.eval (n : ℤ))} := by
  sorry

/-- If the degree `k` of `f` is larger than or equal to `9`, and `f n` has no fixed `(k - 2)`-th
power divisors other than `1`, then the set of `n` such that `f n` is `(k - 2)`-th power free has
infinitely many elements. This result is proved in [Br11]. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_978.variants.sub_two {f : ℤ[X]} (hi : Irreducible f) (hd : 9 ≤ f.natDegree)
    (hp : ∀ (p : ℕ), p.Prime → ∃ n : ℕ, ¬ (p : ℤ) ^ (f.natDegree - 2) ∣ f.eval (n : ℤ)) :
    {n : ℕ | Powerfree (f.natDegree - 2) (f.eval (n : ℤ))}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
If $k > 3$ (and $k \neq 2^l$), then are there infinitely many $n$ for which $f(n)$ is
$(k-2)$-power-free?

This was disproved by the DeepMind prover agent.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
formal_proof using formal_conjectures at "https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/3b5d6ac2555cd63b83d418c29ff040876be9dee0/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/978.lean#L64"]
theorem erdos_978.variants.allow_fixed_divisors : answer(False) ↔
    ∀ {f : ℤ[X]}, Irreducible f → f.natDegree > 3 →
    (¬ ∃ l : ℕ, f.natDegree = 2 ^ l) → 0 < f.leadingCoeff →
    (¬ ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, (p : ℤ) ^ (f.natDegree - 1) ∣ f.eval (n : ℤ)) →
    {n : ℕ | Powerfree (f.natDegree - 2) (f.eval (n : ℤ))}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
If $k>3$ (and $k \neq 2^l$), and for all primes $p$ there exists $n$ such that $p^{k-2}\nmid f(n)$,
then are there infinitely many $n$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-2)$-power-free?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_978.parts.ii : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ {f : ℤ[X]}, Irreducible f → f.natDegree > 3 →
    (¬ ∃ l : ℕ, f.natDegree = 2 ^ l) → 0 < f.leadingCoeff →
    (∀ (p : ℕ), p.Prime → ∃ n : ℕ, ¬ (p : ℤ) ^ (f.natDegree - 2) ∣ f.eval (n : ℤ)) →
    {n : ℕ | Powerfree (f.natDegree - 2) (f.eval (n : ℤ))}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- Does `n ^ 4 + 2` represent infinitely many squarefree numbers? -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_978.parts.iii : answer(sorry) ↔ {n : ℕ | Squarefree (n ^ 4 + 2)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos978

findings.description: The right-hand side includes the hypothesis `(¬ ∃ l : ℕ, f.natDegree = 2 ^ l)`, so it only covers degrees 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, … . Browning's theorem already settles degree ≥ 9, so the Lean question is really only about k ∈ {5, 6, 7}. The problem Erdős posed is open for k ∈ {4, 5, 6, 7, 8}. The source's own special case, 'In particular, does n^4+2 represent infinitely many squarefree numbers?', has degree 4 = 2^2, which this hypothesis excludes. Powers of 2 were excluded only because of the fixed factor 2^{k-1}. That matters for the (k−1)-power-free question and is already covered by the statement's explicit fixed-divisor hypothesis (∀ p prime, ∃ n, ¬ p^{k-2} ∣ f n). The two readings can differ in truth value. Take a quartic (or degree-8) f with no fixed square (resp. 6th-power) prime divisor that has only finitely many squarefree (resp. 6-free) values. Then the source's answer is 'no', while the right-hand side of parts.ii can still be true. parts.iii covers the single polynomial n^4+2, but no statement in the file covers general quartics or degree-8 polynomials. The erdosproblems.com preamble does literally say '(and suppose that k≠2^l for any l≥1)' for the whole problem. The Lean follows that literal reading, which is why I rate this questionable rather than a clear misformalization.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/978 (current, edited 31 Mar 2026): 'Let f∈ℤ[x] be an irreducible polynomial of degree k>2 (and suppose that k≠2^l for any l≥1) … If k>3, and for all primes p there exists n such that p^{k-2}∤f(n), then are there infinitely many n for which f(n) is (k-2)-power-free? In particular, does n^4+2 represent infinitely many squarefree numbers?' Erdős's original [Er65b, p.219] (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1965-17.pdf) attaches the exception only to the (k−1) result: 'I proved [37] that if k > 2 then f(x) represents infinitely many (k-1)-th power-free integers, the only exception being that if k = 2^l then it may happen that f(n) ≡ 0 (mod 2^{k-1}) for all n … I could prove nothing about the representation of (k-2)-th power-free numbers, for example, I cannot show that n^4 + 2 represents infinitely many squarefree numbers.' [Er81h, p.178] (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1981-33.pdf): 'It seems hopeless at present to extend this result to quartic polynomials; in fact there is no quartic polynomial about which we can prove that it represents infinitely many squarefree integers.' A comment on the site's forum thread (Dogmachine, 19 Sep 2025) raised the same point: 'I do not quite understand the restriction on the degree, specially since the last problem IS about a 4th degree polynomial anyway.' The site later added the fixed-divisor condition to part (ii) (history, 2026-03-31) but left the preamble unchanged.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove `(¬ ∃ l : ℕ, f.natDegree = 2 ^ l) →` from `erdos_978.parts.ii`, and '(and $k \neq 2^l$)' from its docstring. The statement's fixed-divisor hypothesis already rules out the 2^{k-2} obstruction. parts.iii then becomes a special case: n^4+2 is Eisenstein at 2, has degree 4 > 3, and f(0) = 2 has no square prime factor. Alternatively, keep the literal version and add a variant without the power-of-2 restriction.

reformulations.difference: The Lean adds a hypothesis `hp` that no prime p has p^{k−1} ∣ f(n) for every n, which the source's first question does not state. It also states Hooley's positive answer as a plain theorem instead of `answer(True) ↔ …`, and counts n ∈ ℕ (including 0) rather than n ≥ 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: `hp` follows from the other hypotheses. An irreducible f ∈ ℤ[X] of positive degree is primitive (Mathlib `Irreducible.isPrimitive`). The fixed divisor d = gcd{f(n)} of a primitive degree-k polynomial divides k!: write f = Σ a_i C(x,i), so d = gcd(a_i); then k!·f/d ∈ ℤ[x], hence d·content(k!f/d) = k!. Also v_p(k!) = (k − s_p(k))/(p − 1), which is ≤ k − 2 unless p = 2 and k is a power of 2. So when k > 2 and k ≠ 2^l, p^{k−1} never divides d. Divisibility for all n ∈ ℕ is the same as for all n ∈ ℤ, by periodicity mod p^{k−1}. Adding or removing the single point n = 0 does not change natural density. So the theorem is exactly the positive answer to 'does the set have positive density?' as posed.

reformulations.difference: The Lean carries the extra hypothesis `¬ ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ ∀ n, p^{k−1} ∣ f n`. Neither the docstring nor the earlier site statement it formalizes (history revision 2026-03-31 12:44:38: 'If k>3 then are there infinitely many n for which f(n) is (k-2)-power-free?') has it. A reader might suspect it should be p^{k−2}, which would turn the statement into the open parts.ii and make answer(False) wrong.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: By the same fixed-divisor argument (the fixed divisor divides k!, and v_p(k!) ≤ k−2 unless p = 2 and k = 2^l), the hypothesis is implied by irreducibility together with degree > 3 and not a power of 2. So the statement is equivalent to the no-fixed-divisor-condition version, which is false. I proved the file's exact statement, `answer(False) ↔ …`, sorry-free in /workspace/review/scratch3.lean; `example : type_of% @Erdos978.erdos_978.variants.allow_fixed_divisors := …` typechecks with axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. The witness is f = X^6+33X^5+21X^4+63X^3+18X^2+24X+48: it is Eisenstein at 3 and monic, has natDegree 6, and satisfies 16 ∣ f(n) for all n (checked by `decide` on ZMod 16), so it is never 4-power-free, while f(0) = 48 has no 5th-power prime factor. So answer(False) is correct. The Lean equivalence itself (the hypothesis being redundant) was not proved.

review.notes:
Per-declaration summary:
- sub_one matches Erdős 1953. His theorem needs k ≥ 3, a primitive f with positive leading coefficient, and for k = 2^l some n with 2^{k−1} ∤ f(n). The Lean is the k ≠ 2^l special case.
- parts.i matches Hooley 1967. The extra fixed-divisor hypothesis is redundant (see reformulations).
- sub_two matches Browning 2011. For irreducible f of degree d, the asymptotic formula for k-free values holds when k ≥ (3d+1)/4, as restated in arXiv:2504.00804 and arXiv:1801.04481. With k = d−2 this is exactly d ≥ 9. Browning needs neither k ≠ 2^l nor a positive leading coefficient. The sign is immaterial anyway: replace f by −f and use `powerfree_neg`. So dropping those preamble hypotheses is correct for this variant.
- allow_fixed_divisors: I proved the full statement sorry-free in Lean (scratch3.lean), confirming answer(False). The counterexample is the one posted on the erdosproblems.com forum (31 Mar 2026).
- parts.iii faithfully states the n^4+2 question.
- Status: the categories (parts.ii and parts.iii open; the rest solved) match the site's OPEN status. They also match the teorth/erdosproblems database. Later papers (Wang–Yi 2025/26, Lapkova–Xiao) still give Browning's k ≥ (3d+1)/4 as the best general result, so part (ii) is still open.

Metadata nit (not a finding): the `formal_proof` on allow_fixed_divisors uses kind `formal_conjectures`, which CONTRIBUTING.md defines as 'formally proved in this repository'. Its link points to a fork (github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures); `lean4` may be the more accurate kind. I did not open that link, because it is a copy of the repository I was told not to consult.

Sourcing: I did not read the Hooley, Browning and Heath-Brown papers themselves (they are paywalled). For those I relied on the site's remarks and the two arXiv restatements. Erdős's own texts ([Er53], [Er65b, p.219], [Er81h, p.178]) were read from the OCR layers of the Rényi Institute scans.
